[0] everyday_reading (E): In maths `|` means 'divides', absolute value or 'or'. In a command line, `A | B` connects A's standard output to B's standard input.
[1] misconception (M) -> RedirectionIsArgument: wrong rule: A redirected (piped) stream shows up in args[]. Right rule: With `A | B`, B's standard input is A's output stream. It is not an argument, and B just reads standard input as if someone were typing it.
[2] inconsistent_trace (T) -> RedirectionIsArgument: Points to LT (A's writes are added to the end of the shared stream and B's reads take from its front, interleaved by the OS). An uneven trace runs A to completion into a file first, or sends B's output back into A. (here mixing in: "a redirected file shows up in args[]")

[0] names_the_element (N): Piping is an operating-system mechanism (`|`) that makes one program's standard output the next program's standard input.
[1] states_the_rule (S): `java RandomSeq 1000 | java Average` specifies that RandomSeq's standard output and Average's standard input are the same stream.

[0] line_by_line_trace (LT): The two programs run together. Each println in A adds a string to the end of the stream, and each read in B removes one from the beginning. The OS decides the interleaving, and the result does not depend on it.
[1] output_prediction (OP): Only the last program's standard output appears. `java RandomSeq 100000 | java Average` prints a single line such as Average is 0.5000499417963857.
[2] one_step_execution (OS): One write by A makes one more item available to B. One read by B consumes it. No file is created.

[0] relation_to_neighbour (R): A pipe has the same effect as `> file` then `< file`, but there is no intermediate file, so the data size is not limited by disk space.
[1] relation_to_neighbour (R): Filters are the components and the pipe is the connector: `A | F1 | F2` passes the stream through each filter in turn.
[2] purpose_of_the_whole (P): Piping composes small programs into a pipeline and removes the limit on stream size.

[0] predict_a_change (C) -> RedirectionIsArgument: Replacing `A | B` with `A > f; B < f` keeps the result. Changing A's output format (e.g. adding a label) breaks B's typed reads.
[1] transfer_to_a_new_program (X): Use a pipe when one program's output is exactly the next program's input and the intermediate data need not be kept. Use redirection to a file when it must be saved or reused.
[2] diagnose_an_error (D): rule broken: The upstream output must match the downstream input format. Kind: run-time exception. Trigger class: A prints labels such as `Average is 0.5`, and B reads them with readDouble(): NumberFormatException on the token `Average`.

wrong: a redirected file shows up in args[] | right: With < data.txt the operating system implements the standard input stream by reading from the file; the program just reads standard input and has no dependence on the source of the input stream.

A filter converts a standard input stream to a standard output stream, and piping is the mechanism that connects filters together.
A pipe A | B connects A's standard output directly to B's standard input, with no file in between.
Piping joins the commands that run two programs, so one program's output becomes the other's input.
